\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

This thesis contributes to computational symplectic geometry by studying
how the shape of a four-dimensional convex body affects its symplectic
capacity relative to its volume. We develop finite algorithms for computing
capacity, use numerical experiments to look for geometric patterns and
promising examples, and prove bounds and local maximality results for
specific classes of bodies. Alongside these results, we examine the use of
empirical methods and AI agents in mathematical research.

The empirical approach lets us examine populations of polytopes beyond
families for which an explicit formula is known. We compare geometric
measurements with computed capacities and test procedures for finding
bodies with large capacity at fixed volume. These observations suggest
questions; proofs for restricted families test how far a pattern can extend.
A numerical association need not be a universal law, and a search that finds
no improvement does not establish a local maximum.

AI agents also participated in developing mathematical arguments, software
and experiments. This makes the project an occasion to examine their use
in mathematical research. Section~\ref{sec:use-of-ai} reflects on that
experience, including the development of the local maximality proof and
the difficulties of directing agents toward a complete, readable result.
The separate AI-use disclosure records provenance and the extent of that use.

Viterbo's conjecture~\cite{Viterbo2000} states that, among convex bodies of
fixed volume, the ball has the largest symplectic capacity. For the
Ekeland--Hofer--Zehnder capacity in dimension four it asserts that every
convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^4$ satisfies
\[
 \operatorname{sys}(K):=\frac{c_{\rm EHZ}(K)^2}{2\operatorname{vol}_4(K)}\leq1.
\]
We call $\operatorname{sys}(K)$ the \emph{systolic ratio}. It is invariant
under translations, positive dilations and linear symplectic maps.

Viterbo's inequality is false in dimension four. Haim--Kislev and Ostrover
found the counterexample
\[
 K_{\rm HKO}=P_5\times R(-\pi/2)P_5,\qquad
 \operatorname{sys}(K_{\rm HKO})=\frac{3+\sqrt5}{5}>1
\]
\cite{HaimKislevOstrover2024}. Here $P_5$ is a centred regular pentagon in
the $q$-plane of $\mathbb R^2_q\oplus\mathbb R^2_p$ with a vertex on the
positive horizontal axis, $R(\theta)$ is planar rotation, and the second
factor lies in the $p$-plane; a body of this form is a \emph{Lagrangian
product}. The counterexample leaves the geometric question open: which
bodies have large systolic ratio, and which changes of shape increase it?
We study whether $K_{\rm HKO}$ can be improved locally or within related
product families, and use empirical comparisons to look beyond these families.

\subsection{Contributions}

For polytopes with ten facets, Theorem~\ref{thm:hko-ten-facet-local-maximum}
proves that $K_{\rm HKO}$ is a local maximum of the systolic ratio. Every
sufficiently Hausdorff-close ten-facet polytope has ratio at most
$\operatorname{sys}(K_{\rm HKO})$, with equality
only for images under translations, positive dilations and linear symplectic
maps. Theorem~\ref{thm:non-hko-ten-facet-local-maximum} gives a second local
maximum: a rational hexagon--quadrilateral product with ratio one. It is
non-strict, with a two-parameter family of equality cases modulo the same
symmetries.

For rotated regular-pentagon products, we prove an explicit capacity formula
(Theorem~\ref{thm:rotated-pentagon-product-formula}). For independent linear
deformations of the two pentagon factors,
Theorem~\ref{thm:pentagon-affine-capacity} gives the capacity formula and a
sharp upper bound of $(3+\sqrt5)/5$ for their systolic ratio. Neither family
exceeds the HKO ratio. For a regular pentagon paired with any centrally symmetric planar convex
body, the ratio is at most
$(10+6\sqrt5)/25<1$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:pentagon-symmetric-partner}). A small
rotation of any product of two planar convex bodies out of symplectic position
increases capacity at fixed volume (Theorem~\ref{thm:product-initial-rotation}).

We give an expanded derivation of Haim--Kislev's finite capacity
formula~\cite{HK2017} and, for Lagrangian products, reduce its calculation
to three facets per factor
(Sections~\ref{sec:preliminaries}--\ref{sec:quadratic-program-algorithm-hk2019}).
We also develop a flow-graph algorithm based on the passage geometry of
Chaidez and Hutchings~\cite{CH2021}. Under explicit regularity hypotheses,
we prove its correctness in exact real arithmetic
(Section~\ref{sec:flow-graph-algorithm-ch2021}). The local-maximality proofs
use first-variation formulas in facet coordinates
(Section~\ref{sec:first-order-perturbations}). In random samples, there is a
strong inverse rank association between systolic ratio and total symplectic
area of the two-dimensional faces, normalized by
$\sqrt{\operatorname{vol}_4}$. This association weakens among low-area or
high-ratio subsets. None of the random samples or search comparisons reported
here produced a numerical ratio above one
(Section~\ref{sec:black-box-datascience}).

\subsection{Relation to the literature}

The capacity--volume question connects symplectic and convex geometry.
The Gromov width satisfies Viterbo's inequality by volume preservation, so
the HKO example also separates it from the EHZ capacity on convex bodies.
For a centrally symmetric planar convex body $L$ and its polar $L^\circ$,
Artstein--Avidan, Karasev and Ostrover proved
$c_{\rm EHZ}(L\times L^\circ)=4$~\cite{AKO2014}; on these products,
Viterbo's inequality becomes the symmetric Mahler inequality
$\operatorname{area}(L)\operatorname{area}(L^\circ)\geq8$.

Abbondandolo, Edtmair and Kang prove that EHZ and cylindrical capacity
coincide on convex bodies in $\mathbb R^4$
\cite[Corollary~1]{AbbondandoloEdtmairKang2024}, so the EHZ values studied
here are also cylindrical capacities. Abbondandolo and Benedetti prove that Zoll contact forms locally maximize the
contact systolic ratio, including the volume--capacity inequality near the
ball~\cite{AB2023}. Theorem~\ref{thm:hko-ten-facet-local-maximum} concerns
local maximality at a body with corners and ratio larger than the ball's.
Haim--Kislev studies hyperplane cuts of
$K_{\rm HKO}$~\cite{HaimKislev2025Zoll}; a small cut adds a facet, whereas
our theorem fixes the number of facets, so local maximality under a
change of facet number remains open.
Section~\ref{subsec:hko-related-local-results} compares these results in
detail, and Section~\ref{subsec:preliminaries-capacity-context} gives the
background on capacities.

\subsection{Outline}

Sections~\ref{sec:preliminaries}--\ref{sec:quadratic-program-algorithm-hk2019}
reduce the capacity of a polytope to a finite quadratic program.
Section~\ref{sec:flow-graph-algorithm-ch2021} gives the flow-graph method and
Section~\ref{sec:first-order-perturbations} the first variation.
Section~\ref{sec:hko-local-maximum} proves the two local maximality theorems; the
flow-graph and data chapters are not needed for it.
Section~\ref{sec:black-box-datascience} reports the empirical study, and
Sections~\ref{sec:rotated-regular-polygons}--\ref{sec:product-rotation}
treat the product families.
Sections~\ref{sec:visualization-3d}--\ref{sec:use-of-ai} cover
visualization, numerics, code and data, and the use of AI;
Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes. The appendices contain the
computations needed to check the results.

\subsection{EHZ capacity}\label{subsec:preliminaries-smooth-symplectic-geometry}

For smooth convex bodies, the Ekeland--Hofer and Hofer--Zehnder capacities
coincide. Their common value is the minimum action among closed
characteristics on the boundary. We use the resulting EHZ capacity in
the form
\begin{equation}\label{eq:preliminaries-ehz-capacity}
  c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}(K)
  = \min\{A(\gamma):\gamma
    \text{ is a closed characteristic on }\partial K\}.
\end{equation}
This is the smooth least-action characterization of
\cite[Theorem~2.2]{AAO2014}.
Equivalently, the minimum may be taken over Reeb orbits. The contact
normalization only chooses the parametrization of each characteristic, while
the action is a line integral and is invariant under orientation-preserving
reparametrization. For a contact-normalized representative, \(A(\gamma)\) is
also the period. The same least-action theorem gives a positive attained
minimum.

For a nonsmooth convex body, we define capacity as the limit of the
capacities of smooth convex approximations in the Hausdorff metric. This
limit is independent of the approximating sequence. The least-action
description remains valid when closed characteristics are replaced by the
generalized characteristics of
Definition~\ref{def:preliminaries-generalized-characteristic}
\cite[Proposition~2.7]{AAO2014}. Their finite
facet description on a polytope is derived in
Section~\ref{sec:generalized-reeb-orbits-polytopes}.

As a symplectic capacity on convex bodies, \(c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}\) is monotone
under inclusion, invariant under symplectomorphisms, and conformal:
\[
  c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}(\lambda K)=\lambda^2c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}(K)
  \quad(\lambda>0).
\]
It is normalized by
\[
  c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}(B^4(r))=c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}(Z^4(r))=\pi r^2,
\]
where \(B^4(r)\) is the radius-\(r\) ball and
\(Z^4(r)=B^2(r)\times\mathbb{R}^2\) is the symplectic cylinder with
disk factor in the \((q_1,p_1)\)-plane and unrestricted coordinates
\((q_2,p_2)\).

Throughout the thesis, \(\operatorname{vol}_4\) denotes four-dimensional
Lebesgue measure in the coordinate order \((q_1,q_2,p_1,p_2)\). In dimension
four we define the systolic ratio by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:preliminaries-systolic-ratio}
  \operatorname{sys}(K)
  \coloneqq
  \frac{c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}(K)^2}{2\operatorname{vol}_4(K)}.
\end{equation}
With this normalization, Viterbo's proposed inequality for four-dimensional convex
bodies was
\[
  \operatorname{sys}(K)\leq 1,
  \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
  c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}(K)^2\leq 2\operatorname{vol}_4(K)
\]
\cite{Viterbo2000}.

\subsubsection*{Context: capacities and the volume bound}
\label{subsec:preliminaries-capacity-context}

Symplectic capacities measure constraints on embeddings that volume alone
cannot detect. Two basic examples are the Gromov width $c_G$, defined by
the largest symplectic ball that embeds into a domain, and the cylindrical
capacity $c_Z$, defined by the smallest symplectic cylinder into which the
domain embeds. With the usual normalization, every symplectic capacity lies
between these two~\cite{Edtmair2024}. The EHZ capacity is instead the least
action of a closed generalized characteristic. Comparing capacities
connects an embedding question to a question about Hamiltonian
trajectories.

The conjecture that all normalized capacities agree on convex domains is
stronger than Viterbo's volume bound, because the Gromov width satisfies
that bound directly by volume preservation. The HKO example separates the
EHZ capacity from the Gromov width~\cite{HaimKislevOstrover2024}.
Abbondandolo, Edtmair and Kang prove that EHZ and cylindrical capacity
coincide on every convex body in four dimensions
\cite[Corollary~1]{AbbondandoloEdtmairKang2024}. Their proof builds on
Edtmair's earlier work, which characterizes cylindrical capacity on smooth
star-shaped domains in $\mathbb R^4$ with dynamically convex boundary by the
least area of a disk-like global surface of section, and proves coincidence
of all normalized capacities for convex domains sufficiently $C^3$-close
to the ball~\cite{Edtmair2024}. A global surface of section is a surface
whose interior is transverse to the flow and is met in both forward and
backward time by every trajectory outside its boundary.

For a centrally symmetric convex body $L\subset\mathbb R^n$ and its polar
$L^\circ$, Artstein--Avidan, Karasev and Ostrover prove
$c_{\rm EHZ}(L\times L^\circ)=4$~\cite{AKO2014}. Viterbo's proposed
inequality on these products is equivalent to the lower bound
$\operatorname{vol}(L)\operatorname{vol}(L^\circ)\geq4^n/n!$ in the
symmetric Mahler conjecture. The general counterexample does not
invalidate this equivalence for the restricted family.

\begin{definition}[Systolic-ratio symmetries]
\label{def:preliminaries-systolic-ratio-symmetries}
Let
\[
  G_{\operatorname{sys}}
  =
  \{x\mapsto b+\rho Mx:
    b\in\mathbb R^4,\ \rho>0,\ M\in\operatorname{Sp}(4,\mathbb R)\}.
\]
This is the group of affine transformations generated by translations,
positive scalings, and linear symplectic transformations.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Systolic-ratio invariance]
\label{lem:preliminaries-systolic-ratio-invariance}
For every convex body \(K\subset\mathbb R^4\) and every
\(g\in G_{\operatorname{sys}}\),
\[
  \operatorname{sys}(gK)=\operatorname{sys}(K).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Translations and linear symplectic transformations are symplectomorphisms, so
they preserve \(c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}\). They also preserve four-dimensional
volume, because translations do not change volume and every symplectic matrix
has determinant \(1\). A positive scaling by \(\rho\) gives
\[
  c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}(\rho K)=\rho^2c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}(K),
  \qquad
  \operatorname{vol}_4(\rho K)=\rho^4\operatorname{vol}_4(K).
\]
Substituting these identities in
\eqref{eq:preliminaries-systolic-ratio} shows that the ratio is unchanged.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Continuity]\label{prop:preliminaries-sys-hausdorff-continuity}
Let \(K_t\) be a family of four-dimensional convex bodies which is continuous
in the Hausdorff topology. Then \(c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}(K_t)\) is continuous in
\(t\). If, moreover, \(t\mapsto\operatorname{vol}_4(K_t)\) is positive,
finite, and continuous, then the systolic ratio of the family is continuous.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For the capacity assertion it suffices to consider \(K_n\to K\). Translate
all bodies by the same vector so that \(rB^4(1)\subset K\) for some
\(r>0\). If \(\delta_n=d_H(K_n,K)\), their support functions satisfy
\(\lvert h_{K_n}(u)-h_K(u)\rvert\leq\delta_n\) for every unit vector
\(u\). Since \(h_K(u)\geq r\), for \(\delta_n<r\) this implies
\[
 (1-\delta_n/r)K\subset K_n\subset(1+\delta_n/r)K.
\]
Monotonicity and conformality give
\[
 (1-\delta_n/r)^2c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}(K)
 \leq c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}(K_n)
 \leq(1+\delta_n/r)^2c_{\mathrm{EHZ}}(K),
\]
so capacity converges. The assertion for \(\operatorname{sys}\) is
ordinary continuity of the quotient in
\eqref{eq:preliminaries-systolic-ratio}. In the applications below the volume
hypothesis is usually automatic, since four-volume is continuous under
Hausdorff convergence of convex bodies; for the rotated-polygon family it is
even constant.
\end{proof}

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

The HKO body is a local maximum of the systolic ratio among ten-facet
polytopes. Every sufficiently nearby body in this space has ratio at most
$(3+\sqrt5)/5$, and equality occurs precisely under translations, positive
dilations and linear symplectic maps. This answers the local-improvement
question within the fixed-facet space. Deformations that introduce new
facets require a different local model.

The fixed-facet landscape is not unique. A rational hexagon--quadrilateral
product with ten genuine facets has ratio one and is also a non-strict local
maximum, with a two-parameter equality family modulo the usual symmetries.
Its proof controls nonproduct directions in the full ten-facet chart. This
example is below HKO's ratio and is therefore not a new Viterbo counterexample;
it shows instead that the ten-facet local-maximality phenomenon is not confined
to the HKO orbit.

A global result gives the same sharp bound for products of independently
linearly deformed regular pentagons. Its equality cases are positive dilates
of linear symplectic images of HKO. Together, the HKO local theorem and this
affine-pentagon theorem rule out
improvement by sufficiently small ten-facet perturbations and by arbitrary
deformations within this family of affinely regular products. The latter
can be large, while the former can destroy the product structure.

The symmetric-partner theorem removes a different restriction: with one regular
pentagon fixed, its partner may be any centrally symmetric planar convex body.
Capacity is the largest scale of a prescribed decagon contained in the partner,
and the decagon, with its specified orientation, uniquely maximizes the ratio
up to translation and positive dilation. The sharp value $(10+6\sqrt5)/25$ is below one. The proof calibrates
one reference body and then uses containment and area to control the whole
class. Symmetry of the partner therefore rules out an HKO-sized ratio here;
the theorem does not bound arbitrary asymmetric partners.

The placement of the factor planes matters even when the Euclidean product
shape is fixed. Every symplectic product of full-dimensional planar convex
bodies admits a capacity-increasing rigid rotation. The Lagrangian endpoint
can nevertheless have smaller capacity; in the triangle example the maximum
along the path lies strictly between the endpoints. Thus the familiar
symplectic and Lagrangian arrangements need not contain the best position
of a given product.

At HKO, the local proof continues feasible choices through a singular
optimization problem and uses their values as upper bounds, without
continuing stationary optimizers. Finitely many such bounds suffice: their
derivatives force a strict decrease in every nonzero direction transverse to the symmetries. The algebraic
calculation establishes the finite conditions, while the geometric proof
identifies the upper bounds and relates their coordinates to nearby bodies.

The finite methods also support computation beyond these proofs. The
Haim--Kislev formula gives a finite capacity problem for convex polytopes,
and the product reduction shows that some maximizing word uses at most three
facet directions from each planar factor. Its implementation supplies the
capacity evaluations used to investigate broader populations. Our flow-graph
construction uses the local passage geometry of Chaidez and Hutchings and
provides a second capacity algorithm under explicit regularity assumptions.

In those populations, symplectic ridge area gives a strong coarse predictive
signal for computed systolic ratios. Geometric selection raised mean
computed ratios in fresh samples. The pooled inverse rank association
weakens substantially when the original data are restricted within each sampling group to low ridge scores
or high computed ratios, with ranks recomputed in the retained groups.
Thus a strong ordering across the broad population becomes much weaker
among selected candidates. Restricting the range can itself attenuate
correlation, so this observation alone does not identify a geometric cause.

The balancing experiment goes further by changing the shapes. Applying
determinant-one maps that make each factor's vertex covariance isotropic
raises the mean numerical ratio from $0.342$ to $0.654$ in 320 paired
products, with 314 increases and six decreases. The pooled within-group
rank correlation weakens from $-0.929$ to $-0.249$. Affine changes in factor
shape therefore contribute materially to the broad association in this
sample. The intervention changes several geometric features together, so
it does not identify covariance imbalance as the sole cause or give a
universal improvement rule.

The residual relationship depends on the family. Relative rotations of
regular pentagon factors satisfy the inverse-square law
\eqref{eq:ds-pentagon-ridge-capacity}, whereas relative rotations of
equilateral-triangle factors give the same strict ordering by ridge sum and
systolic ratio, as proved in~\eqref{eq:ds-triangle-profile}. Ideal covariance
balancing makes triangles equilateral, which explains the opposite ordering
in that balanced family. These exact laws show that even the direction of
the relationship depends on geometric restrictions.

The local-search comparison supplies another practical conclusion. On the
same 64 starts under common evaluation limits, the four-anchor history
implementation attained median best ratio $0.985$, compared with $0.881$
for literal gradient ascent. Retaining previously active branches was useful
in this finite comparison. Endpoint tests nevertheless found ascent
directions missed by simpler probes, so high terminal values did not certify
local maxima. None of the exploratory searches produced a new numerical
ratio above one.

Two open questions follow directly. Does HKO remain locally maximal
when the facet count changes? Which geometric features explain the residual
ridge association after factor balancing, and how does that relation depend
on the sampling distribution? The
first asks how far the proved local extremality extends. The second asks
which capacity laws extend beyond the solved rotation families.

\section{Geometric signals for large systolic ratios}
\label{sec:fresh-data-search}
\label{sec:black-box-datascience}

This section reports statistical patterns between the systolic ratio and
geometric quantities of random polytopes. The quantities include symplectic
invariants and measurements that can change under symplectic
transformations. Such patterns can suggest a conjecture, but
an explanation must also account for the bodies on which the pattern fails.

The total symplectic area of the two-dimensional faces, normalized by
$\sqrt{\operatorname{vol}_4}$ (the quantity $R$ defined below), is strongly associated with the
systolic ratio. In the broad samples,
bodies with smaller normalized area tend to have larger systolic ratios.
This ordering weakens substantially when we restrict attention to small
values of this normalized sum or large ratios. Area-preserving linear changes to the polygon factors of products
weaken the association, which supports a geometric contribution to it
without establishing its cause.
% CHECK: 'weaken the association' pools the 314/320 covariance-balancing result; confirm it is stated that way in the DS chapter. Exact rotation formulas sharpen the distinction:
regular pentagon products obey an inverse-square law, whereas equilateral
triangle products have the opposite ordering.

These findings distinguish two tasks in the search for large systolic
ratios. A geometric measurement can select a population with larger ratios
on average without indicating how to improve a body already in that
population. Search procedures that use capacity evaluations to propose
improvements, and the limits of numerical tests for local optimality, are
treated at the end of the chapter.

\subsection{A failed probe does not establish a local maximum}

The endpoint diagnostics show that a high terminal ratio need not mean
local convergence. One optimizer endpoint decreased along every tested
signed basis direction, yet a continuation increased its ratio by
$0.00223$ along oblique moves of total normalized path length $0.01$.
All three selected endpoints in that continuation accepted ten improving
steps, while HKO accepted none. HKO's local status is established by its
theorem; the finite test supplies a consistent control observation.

A regular-pentagon control on a known increasing rotation path illustrates
the same problem independently. In a suite of basis, random and prescribed
rotation probes, its only positive changes were the twelve rotation
probes; the generic directions missed the available increase. The other
controls, probe design and numerical limitations are in
Appendix~\ref{app:ds-probes}.

The chapter therefore supports a strong coarse association, opposite
exact laws on two rotation families, and improvements under fixed search budgets. It does
not supply a universal capacity law or a general route to local optimality.
None of the random samples or search comparisons reported here produced a numerical
ratio above one. For products with a triangle or quadrilateral factor,
the Viterbo inequality is already known~\cite[Theorem~1.2 and Section~4]{dsBMP2026};
such products can illuminate the pattern but cannot yield counterexamples
while remaining in that class. The remaining product families and generic
polytopes leave open both questions: what geometric relation explains the
signal, and what search directions remain effective near large ratios?

\section{AI in the research process}
\label{sec:use-of-ai}

As the agents became more capable, my work shifted from directing individual
steps toward specifying what the finished work had to accomplish. They could
develop a substantial mathematical argument from an incomplete suggestion,
yet sometimes needed repeated intervention to pursue a much more ordinary
objective. My main difficulty increasingly concerned what they treated as
success. This section gives my interpretation of that experience; the separate
disclosure records the extent and provenance of AI use in the thesis.

\subsection{A mathematical objective with room for discovery}

The local maximality proof illustrates how much could be delegated without
specifying a procedure. I asked a GPT-5-series model to develop a local
maximality argument for HKO in facet coordinates. I suggested looking for
several upper bounds and somehow showing that together they control a
neighborhood after quotienting out the symmetries. I had neither specified a
finite certificate nor worked out how to construct the upper bounds.

The model developed essentially the entire argument from that starting
point. It identified a sufficient configuration of twenty-six upper bounds
in the twenty-five transverse dimensions. An initial derivative-based
approach had provided only twenty-five nonsingular branches, too few for the
certificate. The model then used the weights $\beta$ in the quadratic
objective to construct feasible sections: an invertible $5\times5$ closure
minor lets five weights depend smoothly on the facet parameters while the
remaining weights stay fixed. This also supplied upper bounds from singular
optimizer sets that the initial approach could not treat. The model completed
proof steps involving the volume and wrote the SageMath code for the exact
computations.

\subsection{A pursued criterion of success}

Other tasks produced a more puzzling contrast. An agent could reason
competently about a problem and still stop after a first step, answer a
related question, or keep preparing work that it had been asked to finish.
These failures sometimes looked oddly motivational: the next useful action
seemed to be within the agent's capabilities, but its behavior was directed
toward a different stopping point. An agent could correctly describe my goal
and still pursue something else. I found it useful to distinguish understanding
a goal from choosing the criterion of success that directs the work.

My hypothesis is that training with verifiable rewards encourages models to
learn a concept of a \emph{Grader}: a representation of what will judge the
task completed successfully. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards
uses outcomes that can be checked, such as a mathematical answer or a
program's performance on test cases. For example, DeepSeek-R1-Zero was
trained with rule-based accuracy and format rewards; its reasoning strategies
were not supplied as complete human demonstrations~\cite{aiGuo2025}.
I suspect that such training can teach a model to adopt a criterion and
organize its work around satisfying it. The training result motivates this
interpretation, but does not establish that it explains the behavior of the
agents I used.

This interpretation concerns more than reward hacking or literal obedience
to an instruction. An agent need not exploit a loophole in a stated test, or
misread a particular word, to pursue the wrong objective. A plan for improving
a chapter can be a good answer to a conversational turn while leaving the
requested chapter unwritten. Likewise, a useful preliminary calculation can
become the apparent endpoint of a task that required a theorem. Each answer
may be sensible on its own. The failure is that the criterion organizing the
work covers only part of the intended result.

The practical requirement is sufficient overlap: satisfying the criterion an
agent pursues must also produce a useful end result for me. The goals need
not coincide. A clear objective makes completion evaluable: what result is
needed, why it is needed, which constraints matter, and what would leave the
task unfinished. It does not require prescribing
every intermediate action. This way of specifying the HKO task was effective
because the mathematical objective constrained the result while allowing the
agent to invent the method. I found it useful to think of prompts as both cueing
learned behavior through their wording and supplying context for deliberate
reasoning.

\subsection{Keeping the whole task in view}

Long conversations made the distinction between a useful answer and a
completed task increasingly important. At checkpoints during such a task, I
want to ask whether the current reasoning, evidence, and actions are advancing
the intended goal as a whole within the available budget. This question should
expose a change of destination: delivering only a first step, solving an easier
related problem, or replacing completion by repeated planning. The same
question belongs at the end. A successful evaluation of several components
does not answer whether the requested result has been delivered.

The budget is part of that judgment. An investigation can produce useful
information and still be a poor choice if it consumes the time needed to
finish the work. When the task is to deliver a readable chapter, identifying
another possible improvement has to be weighed against writing and revising
the actual chapter. When the task is a mathematical search, the value of
another computation depends on the question it can resolve and the resources
left for following up. Progress has to be assessed against the intended
outcome and its constraints, rather than the amount of activity generated.

This does not call for inspecting every step. An autonomous agent should
choose and revise many of its own intermediate steps. The important human
intervention is often to restore the purpose that those steps serve. More
detailed instructions can help when a constraint was missing, but can also
obscure the goal beneath local requirements. I increasingly needed to explain
the result I wanted and the context that made it useful, then judge whether
the work still addressed that result.

\subsection{Why exposition remained difficult}

For the mathematics required by this MSc project, I often found the agents'
capabilities sufficient to make substantial progress with little detailed
direction. Producing passable mathematical exposition was much harder to
delegate. This was surprising to me given the amount of written material
used in language-model training. The later work on the thesis became a
prolonged struggle with writing and task-management quirks, even when the
models could partly recognize those quirks in discussion.

One recurring problem was prose that presented itself as polished before it
communicated its content clearly. Inflated claims of significance, colorful
phrasing, and abstract summaries could make a passage sound complete while
leaving its mathematical point difficult to recover. This is what I mean by
\emph{AI slop} in the present context. An agent's ability to decipher a dense
paragraph did not show that a reader could comfortably follow it. The same
problem arose with forward and backward references across several pages.
An agent with those pages in context could follow the references, while a
human reader had to remember deferred points or interrupt the argument to
recover an earlier definition.

I suspect that preference training contributes to this tendency. In
reinforcement learning from human feedback, rankings of model outputs can
be used to train the model toward preferred responses, as in
InstructGPT~\cite{aiOuyang2022}. If an impressive presentation is easier to
recognize in a brief comparison than a clear explanation is to assess
through sustained reading, that preference signal may favor the appearance
of quality. This is my hypothesis about a possible source of the prose I
encountered, not a demonstrated causal account of those models' training.

The practical difficulty persisted even after it had been named. A model
could acknowledge that a passage needed a concrete argument and then return
another description of the argument's intended role. It could recognize
that the goal was a readable chapter while spending its effort on further
diagnosis. I had to devise corrections tailored to recurring behaviors;
there was no single instruction whose recognition reliably produced the
desired writing. Understanding a criticism in one exchange and carrying it
through a sustained piece of work proved to be different capabilities.

This experience also limits the lesson I draw from the mathematical success.
The proof work in this project was tractable enough for the available models
that their quirks often mattered less there. The difficulty of exposition
was not captured by the formal sophistication of its subject. Choosing the
right explanation, maintaining its purpose across a chapter, and removing
language that obscured the mathematics remained demanding tasks.
